---
title: "Netflix Hystrix: Circuit Breaking"
description: "A worked shop microservices lesson."
---

**Course source:** Day 2 §5. **Running system:** Product, Order and User services.

## Why Order needs a circuit breaker

A timeout prevents a single Product call from waiting indefinitely. However, if Product has been failing on almost every request, repeatedly sending more calls wastes capacity. The course introduces Netflix **Hystrix** to reduce repeated failures and provide isolation and fallback.

Think of the circuit breaker as a small state machine:

~~~text
CLOSED --failure threshold--> OPEN
  ^                            |
  |                         wait period
  |                            v
  +----successful probe---- HALF_OPEN
             |
         failed probe -> OPEN
~~~

**Closed** allows requests. **Open** rejects or short-circuits attempts. **Half-open** permits limited tests of recovery. The actual policy should account for sample size, sliding windows, failure/slow-call thresholds and recovery time.

## A fallback must be domain-safe

If Product is unavailable, the shop may show a cached product description. However, it should **not** silently create a financially binding order using an unknown price. A fallback that invents business facts is worse than a clear temporary-unavailable result.

~~~ts
try {
  const product = await productClient.findById(7);
  return placeOrder(product);
} catch {
  throw new ServiceUnavailableException('Please retry later');
}
~~~

This NestJS-style excerpt illustrates explicit failure semantics; it is not a full Hystrix integration.

## Historical versus current tooling

Hystrix and Ribbon are historical components of the supplied course. For new Spring Cloud work, investigate **Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker with Resilience4j**. The idea of closed/open/half-open remains relevant independently of the library.

## Two failure modes to avoid

A breaker with too little traffic may falsely trip from a tiny sample. A breaker that never probes may remain open after the provider recovers. Treat the policy as an operational hypothesis to validate under realistic traffic.

[Current Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker documentation](https://docs.spring.io/spring-cloud-circuitbreaker/reference/index.html).

## Review questions

What failure does this technique address? Which state belongs to the caller and which belongs to the provider? What would you measure to confirm that it works?
